Daniel’s most interesting empirical surprise—“the sphere actually did better than the torus”—is also where the post hides its strongest unexamined assumption: that “boundary shape” is merely geometric, rather than *topological* in the sense that matters for phase fields. A torus supports persistent phase gradients with nonzero winding numbers (you can go around a loop and come back advanced by \(2\pi k\)), which are bona fide conserved/long-lived modes in many oscillator and XY-type models; those modes can block full global synchrony even when local coupling is strong, because the system can settle into a stable traveling wave or multi-domain pattern instead. A sphere, by contrast, has no nontrivial 1-cycles to carry a global winding number; it can still host local defects/vortices, but it has fewer “topological excuses” for getting stuck in global-gradient states. That’s a concrete, testable reframing of the videos: if Daniel measures winding number (on the torus) or tracks defect count and annihilation (on the sphere), he can turn the qualitative “did better” into a mechanistic statement about which invariants the dynamics preserves or slowly relaxes.

The other blind spot is the analogy to Internet congestion control: “locality” in networks is not a manifold with finite light speed so much as a *graph* with heterogeneous propagation and queueing delays, asymmetric routing, and protocol-specific phase response (hosts don’t “flash,” they adjust windows via a particular control law). In coupled-oscillator terms, the coupling function and the delay distribution typically matter at least as much as embedding geometry—time-delay Kuramoto/Winfree variants can flip stability and select traveling waves depending on whether coupling is effectively attractive/repulsive at the operating frequency. Naming that lineage would sharpen the project: this sits squarely in the literature on synchronization with delays and spatial coupling (e.g., the accessible synthesis in [Strogatz, *Sync*](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/181020/sync-by-steven-strogatz/) and the more technical framing in [Pikovsky, Rosenblum & Kurths, *Synchronization*](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/synchronization/00D34F54A54F9C7B1EE66F6EA8B2C8AA)). If Daniel wants the “Earth’s internet” question to survive beyond metaphor, the next step is to replace “sphere vs torus” with “which graph, which delay model, which control law,” and then see whether the same topological/winding intuition reappears as “cycle structure” and “circulating modes” on real network topologies.
